As well as impacting heat flow through the release of enthalpy, the growing solid within the fluid also impacts the flow of fluid and therefore the ability to feed solidification shrinkage. In CFD simulation, this is typically modeled in regimes that are defined by assumptions regarding the coherency of the solid in the mushy zone. The dendritic coherency point is defined as the state at which dendrite tips have fully grown to the point of a fully coherent network. Another way to state this is that the ridgid skeleton of dendrites is fully established while the interdendritic liquid has yet to solidify. A coherent network of dendritic grains creates a restriction to fluid flow because it is a porous or, colloquially, mushy. As the volume of liquid continues to decrease the flow may cross a critical threshold where the interdendritic volume can no longer be “fed” and microporosity may result. Dendritic coherency has not been well studied in U-Mo alloys, but has been defined for many industrial alloys (Arnberg, Chai, and Backerud 1993). With many caveats regarding composition, cooling rate, and grain refinement, the coherency point tends to fall between 10 and 30 % volume fraction. In thermal analysis studies like that performed here, where the liquid volume experiences only minuscule thermal gradients, coherency would be expected to be dominated by the degree of undercooling of the liquid. While undercooling can result in a visible recalescence signal, in practice this can still be difficult to determine without an accurate phase diagram.
